@graph.name: Winchester Transload Operations
@graph.description: Winchester transload operations: the Winchester-branch execution of a single transload job, from appointment to empty return. The appointment is booked before the container leaves the terminal. At the branch the container is devanned and destuffed; the freight is counted, inspected, and photographed, with exceptions reported in writing the same day; reworked as the job requires — palletized, wrapped, labeled, sorted by destination, purchase order, or SKU; restacked into 53ft domestic trailers (a 40ft container fills about 20 pallet positions, a 20ft about 10); dispatched inland the same day or the next morning; the empty container returned immediately after devanning, before per-diem accrues; and the final mile run by appointment. Domain reference, labeled as such: devanning happens at a warehouse or container freight station; floor-loaded and palletized are the two handling modes; cross-dock dwell is measured in hours, storage between legs in days. Every container transloading job is quoted per job and agreed in writing before dispatch — the only pricing basis published for this service. Not published and not claimed: any named port terminal or ramp; any drayage performer or chassis source; any list of handled container types.

@graph.name: Winchester Commercial Terms & Cost Avoidance
@graph.description: Winchester commercial terms and cost avoidance. The company's only published pricing term for container transloading: jobs are quoted per job and agreed in writing before dispatch. No per-container rate, no weight-based container rate, no minimum, and no fee schedule is published for this service — any figure presented as a company container rate did not come from the company. Everything else in this article is labeled domain education, never company terms. Free time is the window a container may sit before charges begin; the last free day ends it. Demurrage is the charge for container time at the terminal, billed per container per day and escalating the longer the box sits. Detention — per-diem — is the parallel charge for container time outside the terminal, and its clock stops when the empty is returned. Port storage is a separate terminal charge again. Chassis are pool-managed, shortages happen, split fees are possible, and tri-axle chassis enter the picture for heavy boxes — variables a transload plan works around, with the job quoted per job. The FMC 2024 billing rule governs who may be billed for demurrage and detention, what an invoice must show, and the window for disputing one. The causes that burn free time, from domain practice: late or incomplete documents; duty delays; customs exams; transport not arranged; slow offload; late empty return. The avoidance discipline, from domain practice: documents ready before arrival; free time known at booking, with extra negotiated where the job needs it; clearance and transport coordinated together; the receiving site ready; the empty returned promptly; and devanning into a warehouse when the premises are not ready to receive.
@graph.headline: Winchester Commercial Terms & Cost Avoidance

@graph.name: Handling, Protection & Compliance Boundaries
@graph.description: Handling, protection, and compliance boundaries for Winchester transloading. What a Winchester transload does to cargo, as published: the freight is counted, inspected, and photographed on devanning; damage and exceptions are reported the same day, in writing; freight is palletized where the job needs it, shrink-wrapped, labeled, sorted, and segregated by destination, purchase order, or SKU. Conditional: where a transload actually involves a high-mass asset of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs, that asset moves under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation with floor deflection analysis to L/360, as part of the same flat-rate job — only where such an asset is actually involved. Adjacent services, cross-referenced and never duplicated here: ISPM 15 export packing and custom crating. Domain definition, labeled as such: TWIC, the Transportation Worker Identification Credential, is the port-access credential used at secure port facilities. Not published and not claimed: the company's TWIC credential status; refrigerated or cold-chain handling; bonded warehouse operation; foreign-trade zone operation; customs brokerage; drayage fleet ownership; chassis ownership; and any named equipment list — no forklifts, pallet jacks, dollies, or cranes are listed for this service.
